findings.title: Backup code login and disable flows have no e2e tests
findings.body: The PR introduces backup code generation, login via backup code, and disabling 2FA via backup code across next-auth-options.ts, disable.ts, login.tsx, and DisableTwoFactorModal.tsx. The only backup-code-related test added is clicking the download/copy/close buttons in the post-enable dialog (lines 110-125). There is no e2e test that (1) logs in using a backup code, (2) verifies one-time use so a consumed code cannot log in again, (3) disables 2FA through the new 'Lost access' backup code branch, (4) verifies the IncorrectBackupCode / MissingBackupCodes error paths, or (5) inspects the downloaded file. The TODO at line 12 acknowledges the gap, but for a security-sensitive recovery flow the absence of coverage means regressions (e.g., accidental reuse of a code, broken decryption path, race between TOTP and backup branches) can ship undetected.

findings.title: Backup-codes blob URL is never revoked on close or unmount
findings.body: Line 99 calls URL.createObjectURL(textBlob) and stores the result in state. The only revocation is on line 98 inside handleSetup, which only runs when setup is re-invoked successfully. resetState (lines 71-75) does not revoke the URL and the Dialog's onOpenChange handler does not either, and there is no useEffect cleanup. Every successful 2FA setup that is followed by clicking Close, Cancel, X, or an outside click leaks the blob URL for the lifetime of the page. Combined with resetState not clearing backupCodesUrl (see next finding), the URL also leaks across modal open/close cycles.

findings.title: resetState leaves backupCodes, backupCodesUrl, dataUri and secret populated
findings.body: resetState only clears password, errorMessage and step. backupCodes (the in-memory list of plain codes), backupCodesUrl (the blob URL), dataUri (QR image) and secret (TOTP secret) remain. After Cancel/Close the next render of the dialog can therefore briefly render data that no longer matches the database, and the QR image / secret remain in the DOM and in memory until the component is remounted. The blob URL is not revoked (see companion finding), so it persists as a live object URL even after reset.

findings.title: Making PasswordField required can break 2FA disable for non-CAL users
findings.body: PasswordField now declares required when it is shown. The disable endpoint at apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts intentionally skips password verification for non-CAL identity providers (the guard `user.identityProvider === IdentityProvider.CAL` on line 40). If any caller of DisableTwoFactorModal renders it with disablePassword={false} (the default) for a SAML/Google user, that user will be asked for a password they do not have and will be unable to submit the form even though the API would have accepted the disable. The PR does not audit or update call sites of this modal, so this is a likely regression for non-CAL users trying to disable 2FA (including via the new 'Lost access' backup-code branch).

findings.title: Clipboard write rejection is silently ignored
findings.body: navigator.clipboard.writeText(backupCodes.map(formatBackupCode).join("\n")) returns a promise that can reject (insecure context, denied permission, document not focused). The handler ignores the promise and unconditionally shows the success toast `backup_codes_copied`. Users on browsers/contexts without clipboard API permission see a misleading success message while nothing was copied.

findings.title: missing_backup_codes message is misleading and leaks account state
findings.body: When the server returns MissingBackupCodes, the login UI shows t("missing_backup_codes") = "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." In the login flow the user has not yet authenticated, so directing them to settings is not actionable, and the message distinguishes users who have backup codes from those who do not - a small information leak about account state that is otherwise collapsed into a generic error.

findings.title: Backup code consumption is not atomic; same code can authorize two sessions
findings.body: After matching the code, the entry is nullified in the in-memory array and the encrypted blob is written back via a single prisma.user.update. There is no transaction or optimistic check. Two concurrent authorize() calls presenting the same backup code can both read the original array, both nullify index N, and both persist - the second call sees an apparently-valid code and authenticates. The window is small in practice (single user/device), but it directly violates the 'one-time use' guarantee that backup codes are sold on, and is worth a note.
